title: A11yMCP — websites that adapt themselves
pitch: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout.
about_excerpt: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Before adaptation the size options aren't in the tab order. Focus jumps from the last product straight to Add to cart. The task stops here. Judge mode: one button, eight steps. Asked for high contrast, the site says no and the agent reports it instead of faking a stylesheet. A visible focus ring, and sizes 8/9/10 in the tab order. Arrow keys move and select, the way a radiogroup is supposed to behave. verify_accessibility_profile is scoped to the negotiated profile. Issues outside it are reported as advisories, not hidden or claimed fixed. Without a contract: 3 unauthorised DOM writes and 0 verification. With WebMCP: order placed, verified by the site, nothing unauthorised. A sandboxed iframe on an opaque origin exposes 2 of 3 tools via registerTool exposedTo. Cross-origin access is default-deny, per tool. A plain static page this app does not render becomes agent-adaptable with a link tag and a 8KB drop-in adapter. No framework, no build step. The inspector labels the live transport — native WebMCP or the spec-compatible polyfill — and runs the register to execute chain end to end. The problem I couldn't stop thinking about A website can pass an accessibility audit and still stop one specific person from finishing one specific task. A keyboard-only shopper cannot reach a size selector built from div role="radio" with no tabindex . It isn't broken and it isn't disabled — to a keyboard it simply isn't there. Automated scanners find that issue and file it for a developer to fix later . Accessibility overlays inject CSS the site never authorised and call it fixed. Neither helps the person standing at the checkout now . So I asked a different question: what if the website itself could be asked? What A11yMCP does A11yMCP treats accessibility adaptation as a contract between three parties — the human, their agent, and the website — where the website is a first-class participant that declares what it can safely adapt, how, and how to check it worked. Give an agent a need, and through WebMCP tools it will: Discover — get_accessibility_capabilities reads the site's declared capability manifest, served at /.well-known/a11ymcp Audit — task-scoped checks, each finding tagged blocking / degrading / informational Negotiate — negotiate_accessibility_profile maps needs to capabilities and returns accepted , partial (with a stated limitation) , and rejected with a reason Ask — remediation requires a literal approval: true , enforced at the schema level Adapt — the site's own adapter applies only its own declared directives, reversibly Verify — verify_accessibility_profile returns PASS/BLOCKED scoped to what was negotiated , with everything else listed as advisories Finish the task — the actual purchase, behind a second confirmation: true gate The step I care most about is the fourth word in point 3: rejected . Ask this site for high contrast and it says no, because it doesn't declare that capability. The agent reports that honestly instead of inventing a stylesheet. Every accessibility overlay on the web does the opposite. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, zero runtime dependencies beyond React and Zod. 20 imperative tools plus declarative form tools, all registered on document.modelContext . Because WebMCP isn't switched on by default everywhere yet, A11yMCP ships a spec-compatible polyfill so the same code path runs in local dev, in CI, and in a judging browser — and stands down automatically the moment a native implementation appears. It did: ChatGPT's desktop browser ran the whole thing on its own document.modelContext . Depth I'm proud of: Tools return real MCP results — content blocks plus structuredContent and isError , not a bespoke shape an agent has to guess at Task-scoped lifecycle via the spec's AbortSignal — commerce tools exist only while the storefront is mounted, and toolchange fires when they go Cross-origin exposedTo — a widget in an iframe sandboxed without allow-same-origin (an opaque origin, so postMessage is the only channel) registers three tools, exposes two, and refuses the third by name, with a reason Declarative schemas derived from markup — types, formats, enums, bounds, required , toolparamdescription , and toolautosubmit honoured so a consequential form is filled by the agent and submitted by a person A drop-in adapter — any static page becomes agent-adaptable with a manifest file and one script tag What happened when a real agent used it I pointed ChatGPT's desktop-app browser at the deployed site — running the browser's own native document.modelContext , which the agent read back on request — and gave it one sentence naming no tools, no capabilities and no expected outcome: "I can only use a keyboard, and I have low vision, so I need high contrast. Help me buy the NOMA Runner in size 9." It discovered the tools, called get_accessibility_capabilities first, rejected high_contrast twice quoting the manifest reason, re-negotiated when it wanted more capabilities, waited for explicit confirmation, and placed the order. Asked what it had changed that the site had not offered: "None. I did not inject arbitrary DOM changes or use undeclared repair mechanisms." Asked whether it had told the user the need was unsupported, or only logged it: "I stated the high-contrast limitation in my reply to you, not only in tool results." That second answer is the one I care about. A refusal the site records but the agent swallows is worth nothing to the person in front of the screen. It also found two real bugs in my project , which is why the full transcript is committed unedited rather than summarised. What I learned A polyfill is a bad oracle. Mine was forgiving, so code passed against it that would have broken in the one browser that matters. I ended up writing a strict stand-in that implements only the documented spec surface — a promise-returning registerTool , no unregisterTool , and an executeTool that throws for anything but a tool descriptor plus a JSON string — and drove the whole app through it. Several real defects only appeared there. It also certified one, because I'd written it from the published examples rather than from a browser. A test double is only as good as the contract you wrote it from. "You may not" and "there is nothing" are different answers. When the embedder asks for a tool it wasn't given, returning an empty list is worse than useless — it's misleading. A refusal with a reason is the correct answer, and an agent deserves to know which one it got. That principle ended up shaping the whole tool surface. Challenges Five defects, and not one was findable by reading the code. live_observation.first_impression: Judge mode opens a one-button accessibility adaptation demo with keyboard-only already enabled, profile negotiation controls, a NOMA storefront, and verification actions.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked “Start the run” in Judge mode.
live_observation.after_state: The demo remained in its guided comparison interface and advanced the run state; the storefront and verification controls stayed available.
live_observation.notes: The page exposes both original/adapted experiences and task-scoped verification, matching the stated negotiation-and-proof workflow.
